q: The SI unit of electric current, the ampere, is equivalent to:
x: Current is the rate of flow of charge, I = Q/t, so 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹. A joule per coulomb is the volt, and a coulomb per volt is the farad.

q: The SI unit of resistivity is:
x: From R = ρL/A, ρ = RA/L, which has units Ω × m² / m = Ω m.

q: The emf of a cell is defined as the:
o: Energy converted into electrical energy per unit charge passing through the cell
Force with which the cell pushes electrons round the circuit
Charge stored in the cell per unit potential difference
Current delivered by the cell when it is short-circuited
x: Emf is energy supplied per coulomb (E = W/q), measured in volts. Despite its name it is not a force, and charge per volt is capacitance.

q: A steady current of 3 A flows through a wire for 2 minutes. How much charge passes any cross-section of the wire?
x: Q = It = 3 × 120 = 360 C. Using t = 2 s instead of 120 s gives the tempting 6 C.

q: A uniform wire of resistance R is stretched so that its length doubles while its volume stays the same. Its new resistance is:
x: Doubling the length at constant volume halves the cross-sectional area. R = ρL/A becomes ρ(2L)/(A/2) = 4R; forgetting the change in area gives 2R.

q: A battery of emf 12 V and internal resistance 1 Ω is connected to a 5 Ω resistor. The terminal potential difference of the battery is:
x: I = E/(R + r) = 12/6 = 2 A, so V = E − Ir = 12 − 2 = 10 V. The 2 V is the lost volts inside the battery, not the terminal p.d.

q: A current of 1.6 A flows in a metal wire. How many electrons pass a point in the wire each second? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
x: Charge per second is 1.6 C, so n = Q/e = 1.6 / (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 10¹⁹ electrons.

q: Two wires of the same material and the same length are compared. Wire Q has twice the diameter of wire P. If P has resistance R, Q has resistance:
x: Area depends on diameter squared, so Q has four times the area. Since R ∝ 1/A, Q has resistance R/4; using diameter instead of area gives R/2.

q: A very high-resistance voltmeter is connected across the terminals of a cell with nothing else connected. The voltmeter reads (almost exactly) the:
o: Product of emf and internal resistance
Half of the emf of the cell
x: Almost no current flows, so Ir ≈ 0 and V = E − Ir ≈ E. This is how the emf of a cell is measured on open circuit.

q: In the external circuit connected to a cell, which statement about the direction of current is correct?
o: Conventional current and electron flow both go from the positive terminal to the negative terminal
Conventional current flows from the negative terminal to the positive terminal, opposite to the electron flow
Electrons flow from the positive terminal to the negative terminal, the same way as conventional current
Conventional current flows from the positive terminal to the negative terminal, opposite to the electron flow
x: Conventional current is taken as the flow of positive charge, from + to − outside the cell. Electrons are negative and actually move the other way, from − to +.

q: The resistivity of a metal wire depends on:
o: The material of the wire and its temperature
The length of the wire only
The cross-sectional area of the wire only
Both the length and the cross-sectional area of the wire
x: Resistivity is a property of the material at a given temperature. Resistance changes with length and area, but resistivity does not.

q: A car battery must have a very low internal resistance mainly because:
o: The starter motor draws a very large current, and a high internal resistance would waste most of the emf as lost volts
A low internal resistance makes the emf of the battery larger
A low internal resistance stops the battery from producing any heat
The battery must deliver alternating current to the starter motor
x: Lost volts Ir is large when I is large, so for a starter motor's big current r must be tiny to keep the terminal p.d. high. Internal resistance does not change the emf, and some heating still occurs.

q: A current is described as steady when:
o: The rate of flow of charge through any cross-section does not change with time
The charges in the conductor are at rest
The current reverses its direction at regular intervals
The potential difference across the conductor keeps increasing
x: A steady current means the same charge passes per second at every instant, so I is constant in time. Charges at rest give no current, and a current that reverses regularly is alternating.

q: The SI unit of the temperature coefficient of resistivity (α) is:
x: α = (ρt − ρ0)/(ρ0 t) is a fractional change per degree, so the resistance or resistivity units cancel and α is measured in K⁻¹ (per kelvin).

q: A cell of emf 1.5 V has a terminal potential difference of 1.2 V when it delivers a current of 0.3 A. Its internal resistance is:
x: Lost volts = 1.5 − 1.2 = 0.3 V, so r = 0.3 / 0.3 = 1 Ω. Dividing 1.2 V by 0.3 A gives 4 Ω, which is the external resistance.

q: In an electrolyte such as copper sulphate solution, the electric current is carried by:
o: Positive and negative ions moving in opposite directions
x: In electrolytes the charge carriers are ions: positive ions move towards the cathode and negative ions towards the anode. Free electrons are the carriers in metals.

q: The resistance of a metal conductor increases when it is heated because:
o: The number of free electrons in the metal increases
The length of the conductor shrinks on heating
The atoms vibrate with larger amplitude, so free electrons collide with them more often
The electrons gain mass at higher temperature
x: Heating makes the lattice atoms vibrate more strongly, so drifting electrons are scattered more often and resistivity rises. In metals the number of free electrons stays almost the same.

q: For a cell, terminal potential difference (vertical axis) is plotted against the current drawn (horizontal axis). The graph is a straight line sloping downwards. The magnitude of its gradient equals the:
x: V = E − Ir has the form y = c − mx, so the vertical intercept is E and the gradient is −r. The external resistance varies from point to point along the line.

q: A steady current flows through a metal wire whose cross-section becomes narrower along part of its length. Compared with the thick part, the narrow part has:
o: The same current and a lower drift speed of electrons
A larger current and the same drift speed of electrons
A smaller current and a higher drift speed of electrons
The same current and a higher drift speed of electrons
x: Charge cannot pile up, so the same current passes every section. Since I = nAev, a smaller area A needs a larger drift speed v to carry the same current.

q: Which of the following materials has a negative temperature coefficient of resistance?
x: In semiconductors like germanium, heating frees more charge carriers, so resistance falls as temperature rises. Copper, silver and aluminium are metals with positive coefficients.

q: A cell of emf 6 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is short-circuited by a thick copper wire of negligible resistance. The current is about:
x: With R ≈ 0, I = E/r = 6 / 0.5 = 12 A. Multiplying emf by r gives 3 A instead.

q: A charge of 120 C flows steadily through a lamp in 1 minute. The current in the lamp is:
x: I = Q/t = 120 / 60 = 2 A. Forgetting to change minutes to seconds gives 120 A.

q: A wire has a resistance of 10 Ω at 0 °C. Its temperature coefficient of resistance is 4 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹. Its resistance at 50 °C is:
x: Rt = R0(1 + αt) = 10 × (1 + 4 × 10⁻³ × 50) = 10 × 1.2 = 12 Ω. Leaving out the factor R0 in the increase gives 10.2 Ω.

q: When a cell with internal resistance delivers a current, which statement is correct?
o: The terminal p.d. becomes greater than the emf
The emf of the cell falls to zero
All the energy supplied by the cell is delivered to the external circuit
Some energy is dissipated as heat inside the cell, so the terminal p.d. is less than the emf
x: Part of the emf is used to drive current through the internal resistance (lost volts Ir), which heats the cell. So V = E − Ir is less than E.

q: An electric heater and an electric iron work mainly on which effect of electric current?
x: When current passes through a resistor, electrical energy is converted into heat (Joule heating). Heaters and irons use this heating effect.

q: A wire 2 m long has a cross-sectional area of 1 mm² and is made of a metal of resistivity 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. Its resistance is:
x: 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m², so R = ρL/A = 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ × 2 / 10⁻⁶ = 3.2 × 10⁻² Ω. Taking 1 mm² as 10⁻³ m² gives 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ Ω.

q: Which statement about emf and terminal potential difference is correct?
o: Emf and terminal p.d. are always equal for any cell
Terminal p.d. is larger than emf whenever a cell supplies current
Emf is measured in joules and terminal p.d. in volts
Emf exists even when no current flows, but terminal p.d. depends on the current drawn
x: The emf is fixed by the cell's chemistry, while the terminal p.d. falls as current rises (V = E − Ir). Both are measured in volts.

q: A current of 1 A in a metal wire corresponds to about how many electrons passing a point every second? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
x: 1 A means 1 C per second, so n = 1 / (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons per second.

q: Alloys such as manganin and constantan are used to make standard resistors mainly because they have:
o: A very large temperature coefficient of resistance
A very small temperature coefficient of resistance
x: Their resistance hardly changes with temperature, so the value of a standard resistor stays reliable. Resistivity is never zero or negative for these alloys.

q: A battery of emf 9 V and internal resistance 1 Ω is connected to a 2 Ω resistor. How much power is wasted as heat inside the battery?
x: I = 9/(2 + 1) = 3 A, so power in r = I²r = 9 × 1 = 9 W. The 18 W is the power in the 2 Ω load and 27 W is the total power EI.

q: A copper wire of cross-sectional area 1 mm² carries a current of 8 A. It has 5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per m³. Taking e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the drift speed of the electrons is:
x: I = nAve, so v = I/(nAe) = 8/(5 × 10²⁸ × 10⁻⁶ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 8/(8 × 10³) = 1 × 10⁻³ m s⁻¹, with 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m². Taking 1 mm² as 10⁻³ m² gives 10⁻⁶; leaving the area as 1 m² gives 10⁻⁹.

q: A resistor is connected to a supply of fixed potential difference. When its resistance is increased by 2 Ω, the current falls from 3 A to 2 A. The original resistance was:
x: V = IR is the same both times: 3R = 2(R + 2), so R = 4 Ω (and V = 12 V). Check: 12/6 = 2 A. Giving the new resistance gives 6 Ω; 12 is the supply voltage, not a resistance.

q: A carbon resistor has colour bands yellow, violet, orange and gold, in that order. Its resistance is:
x: Yellow = 4, violet = 7, orange = multiplier 10³, gold = ±5% tolerance: 47 × 10³ Ω = 47 kΩ ± 5%. Reading orange as a third digit gives 473 Ω; silver, not gold, means ±10%.

q: A metal wire has resistance R₀ at 0 °C and a temperature coefficient of resistance of 4 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹. Assuming R = R₀(1 + αt) holds, its resistance becomes 2R₀ at:
x: 2R₀ = R₀(1 + αt) gives αt = 1, so t = 1/(4 × 10⁻³) = 250 °C. Adding 273 to the answer gives 523, which is the kelvin value, not the Celsius one.

q: A battery of emf 12 V and internal resistance 2 Ω is connected to an external resistor whose value is chosen to take the maximum possible power. That maximum power is:
x: Maximum power is delivered when R = r = 2 Ω: I = 12/4 = 3 A and P = I²R = 9 × 2 = 18 W (= E²/4r). Using E²/r gives 72 W; forgetting the internal resistance in the current gives 36 W.

q: A lamp is rated 100 W at 220 V. If it is connected to a 110 V supply and its resistance stays the same, the power it takes is:
x: P = V²/R, so with R fixed P ∝ V²: halving V gives ¼ of the power, 100/4 = 25 W. (R = 220²/100 = 484 Ω, and 110²/484 = 25 W.) Taking P ∝ V gives 50 W.

q: Kirchhoff's second rule (the loop rule: the sum of emfs round a closed loop equals the sum of the IR drops) follows from the law of conservation of:
x: Going round a closed loop a charge returns to the same potential, so the energy it gains from emfs equals the energy it loses in resistors: conservation of energy. The junction (first) rule comes from conservation of charge.

q: At a junction, currents of 5 A and 3 A flow in along two wires and 2 A flows out along a third wire. The current in the fourth wire at the junction is:
x: By Kirchhoff's first rule, total current in = total current out: 5 + 3 = 2 + I, so I = 6 A flowing out of the junction. Adding all three numbers gives 10 A.

q: A 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor are connected in parallel, and this pair is connected in series with a 4 Ω resistor across a 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance. The current in the 6 Ω resistor is about:
x: 6 Ω ∥ 3 Ω = 2 Ω, total = 6 Ω, so the battery current is 2 A. The p.d. across the pair is 2 × 2 = 4 V, so the 6 Ω carries 4/6 ≈ 0.67 A and the 3 Ω carries 1.33 A. 2.0 A is the total current.

q: A cell of emf 12 V and a cell of emf 4 V are connected in series so that their emfs oppose each other, in a loop whose total resistance is 4 Ω. The current in the loop is:
x: With the emfs opposing, the net emf is 12 − 4 = 8 V, so I = 8/4 = 2 A by the loop rule. Adding the emfs as if they aided gives 16/4 = 4 A.

q: Between junctions X and Y there are three parallel branches: cell P (12 V) with a 2 Ω resistor, cell Q (6 V) with a 2 Ω resistor, and a third 2 Ω resistor alone. Both positive terminals face X. Ignoring internal resistance, the current in the third resistor is:
x: Loops: 12 = 2I₁ + 2I₃ and 6 = 2I₂ + 2I₃, with I₃ = I₁ + I₂. Adding: 18 = 2I₃ + 4I₃, so I₃ = 3 A (then I₁ = 3 A, I₂ = 0). Adding 12/2 and 6/2 while ignoring the third resistor gives 9 A.

q: A 4 Ω and a 12 Ω resistor are connected in parallel, and a total current of 2 A enters the combination. The current in the 4 Ω resistor is:
x: 4 ∥ 12 = 3 Ω, so the p.d. across both is 2 × 3 = 6 V and the 4 Ω carries 6/4 = 1.5 A (the 12 Ω carries 0.5 A, total 2 A). Giving the larger share to the larger resistor gives 0.5 A.

q: A cell of emf 3 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω drives a current of 0.5 A through an external resistor R. The value of R is:
x: Loop rule: E = I(R + r), so 3 = 0.5(R + 0.5), R + 0.5 = 6 and R = 5.5 Ω. Ignoring the internal resistance gives 6 Ω; adding it instead of subtracting gives 6.5 Ω.

q: Two identical cells, each of emf 2 V and internal resistance 1 Ω, are connected in parallel (positive to positive) and then connected across a 1.5 Ω resistor. The current in the resistor is:
x: In parallel, identical cells give emf 2 V and internal resistance 1 × 1/(1 + 1) = 0.5 Ω, so I = 2/(0.5 + 1.5) = 1.0 A. Adding the emfs as well gives 2.0 A; putting the cells in series gives 4/3.5 ≈ 1.14 A.

q: In applying Kirchhoff's loop rule, when a resistor R carrying current I is crossed in the same direction as the current, the potential:
x: Conventional current flows from higher to lower potential through a resistor, so going with the current the potential falls by IR (written −IR in the loop equation). Crossing it against the current gives +IR.

q: Three 6 Ω resistors are connected so that two of them are in series with each other and this pair is in parallel with the third. The equivalent resistance is:
x: The series pair is 6 + 6 = 12 Ω; 12 Ω ∥ 6 Ω = 12 × 6/18 = 4 Ω. All three in series gives 18 Ω; all in parallel gives 2 Ω; one in series with a parallel pair gives 9 Ω.

q: A battery of emf 12 V and internal resistance 1 Ω is connected across a 3 Ω and a 6 Ω resistor that are in parallel with each other. The current in the 6 Ω resistor is about:
x: 3 ∥ 6 = 2 Ω, so total resistance = 3 Ω and I = 12/3 = 4 A. Terminal p.d. = 12 − 4 × 1 = 8 V, so the 6 Ω carries 8/6 ≈ 1.33 A (and the 3 Ω 2.67 A). Ignoring the internal resistance and the 3 Ω gives 12/6 = 2 A.

q: A cell of emf 6 V (internal resistance 1 Ω) and a cell of emf 3 V (internal resistance 0.5 Ω) are connected in series, aiding each other, across a 3 Ω resistor. The current in the circuit is:
x: Loop rule: I = (6 + 3)/(3 + 1 + 0.5) = 9/4.5 = 2 A. Ignoring the internal resistances gives 3 A; treating the emfs as opposing gives 3/4.5 ≈ 0.67 A.

q: In a Wheatstone bridge, resistors P and Q are in series in one branch and R and S in series in the other, both branches across a battery, with P and R joined to the same battery terminal. A galvanometer joins the P–Q junction to the R–S junction. It reads zero when:
x: At balance the P–Q and R–S junctions are at the same potential, so the p.d. across P equals that across R, giving P/Q = R/S. The other ratios are not equivalent to this condition.

q: In a Wheatstone bridge, P and Q are in series in one branch and R and S in the other, with P and R joined to the same battery terminal and the galvanometer between the P–Q and R–S junctions. It is balanced with P = 10 Ω, Q = 20 Ω and R = 15 Ω. The value of S is:
x: At balance P/Q = R/S, so S = QR/P = 20 × 15/10 = 30 Ω. Check: 10/20 = 15/30. Using S = PR/Q gives 7.5 Ω.

q: A Wheatstone bridge has P = 2 Ω and Q = 4 Ω in series in one branch, R = 3 Ω and S = 6 Ω in series in the other, and a 5 Ω galvanometer joining the P–Q junction to the R–S junction. P and R meet at one battery terminal. The equivalent resistance between the battery terminals is:
x: P/Q = R/S = 0.5, so the bridge is balanced and no current flows in the galvanometer; it can be removed. Then (2 + 4) ∥ (3 + 6) = 6 × 9/15 = 3.6 Ω (the same as (2 ∥ 3) + (4 ∥ 6) = 1.2 + 2.4). Adding all four arms gives 15 Ω.

q: In a metre bridge, an unknown resistor X is in the left gap and a 30 Ω standard resistor in the right gap. The balance point is 40 cm from the left end of the 100 cm wire. The value of X is:
x: X/30 = 40/60, so X = 30 × 40/60 = 20 Ω. Inverting the ratio gives 45 Ω; using 40/100 instead of 40/60 gives 12 Ω.

q: On a potentiometer, a standard cell of emf 1.5 V is balanced by 60 cm of the wire. With the same current in the wire, another cell is balanced by 80 cm. The emf of the second cell is:
x: E ∝ balancing length, so E₂ = 1.5 × 80/60 = 2.0 V. Inverting the ratio gives 1.5 × 60/80 ≈ 1.1 V.

q: A potentiometer measures the emf of a cell more accurately than an ordinary voltmeter because, at the balance point:
o: No current is drawn from the cell being tested
The potentiometer wire has no resistance
A large current flows, which reduces errors
x: At balance the galvanometer shows no deflection, so no current flows from the test cell and there is no lost volt across its internal resistance: the full emf is measured. A voltmeter draws some current, so it reads the slightly smaller terminal p.d.

q: A 12 V supply of negligible internal resistance is connected across a 2 kΩ and a 4 kΩ resistor in series, forming a potential divider. A load of 4 kΩ is connected across the 4 kΩ resistor. The p.d. across the load is:
x: The load is in parallel with the 4 kΩ: 4 ∥ 4 = 2 kΩ, so the 12 V divides equally between 2 kΩ and 2 kΩ, giving 6 V. 8 V is the unloaded output, which forgets that the load lowers the lower resistance.

q: On a potentiometer, a cell on open circuit is balanced by 80 cm of wire. When a 6 Ω resistor is connected across the cell's terminals, the balancing length becomes 60 cm. The internal resistance of the cell is:
x: E ∝ 80 and the terminal p.d. V ∝ 60; r = R(E − V)/V = R(l₁ − l₂)/l₂ = 6 × 20/60 = 2 Ω. Dividing by l₁ instead of l₂ gives 6 × 20/80 = 1.5 Ω; inverting the ratio gives 18 Ω.

q: A potentiometer wire 1 m long has a resistance of 5 Ω. It is connected in series with a 15 Ω rheostat across a driver cell of emf 4 V and negligible internal resistance. The potential gradient along the wire is:
x: I = 4/(5 + 15) = 0.2 A, so the p.d. across the wire is 0.2 × 5 = 1 V and the gradient is 1 V/1 m = 1 V m⁻¹. Taking the whole 4 V across the wire gives 4 V m⁻¹; 3 V is the drop across the rheostat.

q: With the same driver cell, the sensitivity of a potentiometer (its ability to detect small differences of p.d.) can be increased by:
o: Using a longer wire, so the potential gradient is smaller
Using a shorter wire, so the potential gradient is larger
Increasing the current in the wire
Using a galvanometer of lower sensitivity
x: A smaller potential gradient means a small change in p.d. needs a larger change in balancing length, which is easier to measure; a longer wire (or a smaller current) gives this. A larger current or shorter wire raises the gradient and lowers sensitivity.

q: A rheostat with a sliding contact is used as a potential divider across a 10 V supply, the output being taken between one end and the sliding contact. With no load connected, the output p.d. can be varied from:
x: Moving the slider from one end to the other changes the fraction of the rheostat's resistance between the output terminals from 0 to 1, so the output goes from 0 V to the full 10 V. This full range is why a potential divider is used instead of a series rheostat.

q: A Wheatstone bridge (P and Q in one branch, R and S in the other, P and R joined to the same battery terminal) is balanced with P = 10 Ω, Q = 30 Ω, R = 20 Ω and S = 60 Ω. If P and R are interchanged, with Q unchanged, S must be changed to:
x: Now P = 20 Ω and R = 10 Ω, and balance needs P/Q = R/S: 20/30 = 10/S, so S = 30 × 10/20 = 15 Ω. Keeping S at 60 Ω would leave the bridge unbalanced, since 20/30 ≠ 10/60.
